Element E: Application of STEM Principles and Practices

E1. Application of STEM Principles to Design Requirements

● Design Requirements Overview: Briefly list your high-priority design requirements.
1. The design must be able to store up to 200 rolls of 3d printer ﬁlament.

2. Must be able to support up to 200 rolls weighing 1 kg each without breaking or

sinking.

3. Rolls must be organized by their speciﬁc color of ﬁlament, size of rolls, thickness of

ﬁlament, and material of ﬁlament.

4. The design needs to store the rolls out of the way and without interfering with any

other important places/things in the room.

● STEM Applications: Describe how specific STEM principles and practices apply to

these requirements.

○ Example Application: Provide a clear example where a STEM principle

enhances a specific requirement.

Going off of the STEM principle of using falsifiable and testable conditions, and
being able to plan and carry out investigations/experiments, we made each of
these design requirements so that they could be adequately tested in a prototype
to analyze how effective that prototype is, and tweak it if necessary. For design
requirement 1, being able to store 200 rolls of 3D printer filament is easily
testable. We could either use 200 of Mr. L’s filaments to directly test this, or test
this by repeatedly stacking up the few filaments we had from Mr. Gregory’s room
(we had enough filaments to totally fill at least one dowel) on every dowel, and
counting up how many the design could stack in total. The same principles of
investigation and testing apply to requirement 2, where we could again use 200
of Mr. L’s filaments to test whether the prototype breaks.

○ Calculations and Theories: Include relevant calculations or theories that

support the application.

Popper’s falsification theory: https://www.simplypsychology.org/karl-popper.html

For design requirement 1, the prototypes we design would all have 48 dowels of
the same length, so if one dowel were able to support at least 5 dowels (200/48 =
4.167), then we can easily test the requirement using just one dowel. For design
requirement 2, the prototype must be able to support 200 dowels * 1kg/dowel =
200 kg, so one dowel section has to be able to support 200kg/48 = 4.167 kg per
dowel section.

 E2. Substantiation of Proposed Solution with STEM

● Solution Overview: Outline your proposed solution.

All the spools will be stored on the top and side shelves on vertical and horizontal pegs
organized by size, color, or whatever criterion Mr. L wants it to be organized by. The top
shelf will be built from plywood and laid across the existing scaﬀold, which is 144 in x 21 in,
so the actual plywood will need to be about an inch smaller on each side. Vertical pegs will
have a diameter of 1 inch and will be spaced 9 inches apart, making a grid of 16 x 2 vertical
pegs on the shelf, each peg is 16 inches tall. The vertical pegs will serve as long term
storage that can store the bulk of the spools. The horizontal pegs will serve as short term
storage to allow students to have easy access to the spools to swap out with the existing
spools. There will be one horizontal shelf compared to two vertical shelves. The pegs will be
1.5 inches in diameter.

● STEM Justification: Explain how STEM principles substantiate your solution.

○ Detailed Substantiation: Provide a rationale for each STEM principle used,

linking to the solution’s effectiveness.

Mathematical calculations/principles were used to determine the optimal size of the shelf and
the spacing of the pegs. The 9-inch spacing and the 16-inch height of the pegs were calculated
to maximize the number of spools stored while still ensuring ease of access. We similarly used
mathematical calculations to ensure that the (3 separate) plywood beams would be able to
support 200/3 = 67 dowels. According to engineering principles, we designed the peg system to
be modular, allowing for easy reconfiguration as needed.

E3. Expert Review of STEM Applications

● Expert Consultation: Summarize the outcome of expert consultations regarding your

STEM applications.

○ Feedback Summary: Highlight key feedback that influenced further development

or confirmation of your design.

E4. Documentation of Expert Credentials and Review

 ● Expert Credentials: We got the review from Richard Sewall, the Fabrication Lab
Coordinator at Nova Fab Labs, an engineering lab at NOVA community college in
northern Virginia.

● Review Documentation: Provide evidence of expert review, such as excerpts or

summaries.

E5. Impact of Expert Review on Design

● Verification and Corrective Responses: Describe how expert reviews confirmed or led

to modifications in your design.

○ Changes Made: List specific changes made based on expert feedback and the

rationale behind them.

From the expert review we got a good idea of what solution to filament storage they use at
NOVA Fab Labs, and we adapted our design accordingly. We kept the actual storage system
very close to the 3D printers for the convenience of everyone in the classroom in the design.
This decision was based on how they use boxes close to the printers at NOVA Fab Labs, and
the convenience that it brings. We switched to dowels/pipes that can be screwed into the shelf
using 3D printed connections in the design, also for ease of access which was emphasized in
the feedback of the expert reviewer and what they do in their labs. We switched from wooden
dowels to cheaper and lighter PVC, which will work better for our design in this context, and
which is validated by the use of the cheapest possible materials for storage in the labs.

Conclusion Reflect briefly on integrating STEM principles into your project, focusing on the
impact on your design process and the challenges addressed.

 We used STEM principles such as ability to investigate and falsify and using mathematical
calculation and engineering methods to inform the design requirements and the design itself.
These had a large impact on our design requirements in terms of testability, falsifiability, and
measurability. Reflecting on the design requirements, it is clear that good design requirements
should conform to this scientific principle in order to make a good final design. The principles
also had a large impact on the design in terms of the materials used, dimensions used, and the
modularity of the design.

We used several mathematical and scientific principles in our engineering process. The
most essential to the project was gravity. Gravity is what was intended to pull the petals down,
not the motors. The motors were actually only used to hold the petals in place at the top of the
rose and to slow the fall of the petals. We needed the force of gravity on the petals to outweigh
the frictional forces between the fishing wire and the stem when the motors release the wire so
that the petals could accelerate downwards. However, we wanted the petals to be light enough
to create the falling petal effect and to make the drop slower and more dramatic. Weight plays a
dominant role in gravitational force according to the equation F=ma where a is the gravitational
acceleration. Because of this, we balanced the weight of the petal by including small masses in
the fabric while still using a relatively lightweight material. These mechanical principles were
reviewed by field experts from both Duke that had either recently graduated or were currently
participating in their graduate program studies and from theater experts. They gave us
professional feedback that we recorded and took into account while constructing our rose such
as the following points:

-“make the flowers fall pretty. Don’t let them lose their look for function” -stage manager
-“Buttons are hard to push for the stage actors. Especially if it’s the Beast and he’s

wearing gloves” -another stage manager

-“explore other options to not use motors” -a four year graduate named Piper
-a remote is very difficult and intricate so it would be better to find other solutions
-use three motors, one for each scene -Piper
-make carves into dowels to lengthen string -Piper

In order to make the petals fall eloquently we schemed to adjust the motor unspool rate and
speculated the effects of adding fans to blow the falling petals. As for the buttons, we had
decided to send an engineering student to operate the controls as opposed to the actors. We
also considered other options besides motors, the idea of having a motor for each scene, and
carving into the dowels to lengthen string, none of which we implemented in our final plan.

E1. Application of STEM Principles to Design Requirements

● Design Requirements Overview: Briefly list your high-priority design requirements.
1. The design must be able to store up to 200 rolls of 3d printer ﬁlament.

2. Must be able to support up to 200 rolls weighing 1 kg each without breaking or

sinking.

3. Rolls must be organized by their speciﬁc color of ﬁlament, size of rolls, thickness of

Going off of the STEM principle of using falsifiable and testable conditions, and
being able to plan and carry out investigations/experiments, we made each of
these design requirements so that they could be adequately tested in a prototype
to analyze how effective that prototype is, and tweak it if necessary. For design
requirement 1, being able to store 200 rolls of 3D printer filament is easily
testable. We could either use 200 of Mr. L’s filaments to directly test this, or test
this by repeatedly stacking up the few filaments we had from Mr. Gregory’s room
(we had enough filaments to totally fill at least one dowel) on every dowel, and
counting up how many the design could stack in total. The same principles of
investigation and testing apply to requirement 2, where we could again use 200
of Mr. L’s filaments to test whether the prototype breaks.

○ Calculations and Theories: Include relevant calculations or theories that

support the application.

Popper’s falsification theory: https://www.simplypsychology.org/karl-popper.html

For design requirement 1, the prototypes we design would all have 48 dowels of
the same length, so if one dowel were able to support at least 5 dowels (200/48 =
4.167), then we can easily test the requirement using just one dowel. For design
requirement 2, the prototype must be able to support 200 dowels * 1kg/dowel =
200 kg, so one dowel section has to be able to support 200kg/48 = 4.167 kg per
dowel section.

 E2. Substantiation of Proposed Solution with STEM

● Solution Overview: Outline your proposed solution.

All the spools will be stored on the top and side shelves on vertical and horizontal pegs
organized by size, color, or whatever criterion Mr. L wants it to be organized by. The top
shelf will be built from plywood and laid across the existing scaﬀold, which is 144 in x 21 in,
so the actual plywood will need to be about an inch smaller on each side. Vertical pegs will
have a diameter of 1 inch and will be spaced 9 inches apart, making a grid of 16 x 2 vertical
pegs on the shelf, each peg is 16 inches tall. The vertical pegs will serve as long term
storage that can store the bulk of the spools. The horizontal pegs will serve as short term
storage to allow students to have easy access to the spools to swap out with the existing
spools. There will be one horizontal shelf compared to two vertical shelves. The pegs will be
1.5 inches in diameter.

● STEM Justification: Explain how STEM principles substantiate your solution.

○ Detailed Substantiation: Provide a rationale for each STEM principle used,

linking to the solution’s effectiveness.

Mathematical calculations/principles were used to determine the optimal size of the shelf and
the spacing of the pegs. The 9-inch spacing and the 16-inch height of the pegs were calculated
to maximize the number of spools stored while still ensuring ease of access. We similarly used
mathematical calculations to ensure that the (3 separate) plywood beams would be able to
support 200/3 = 67 dowels. According to engineering principles, we designed the peg system to
be modular, allowing for easy reconfiguration as needed.

STEM applications.

or confirmation of your design.

Coordinator at Nova Fab Labs, an engineering lab at NOVA community college in
northern Virginia.

● Review Documentation: Provide evidence of expert review, such as excerpts or

summaries.

E5. Impact of Expert Review on Design

● Verification and Corrective Responses: Describe how expert reviews confirmed or led

to modifications in your design.

○ Changes Made: List specific changes made based on expert feedback and the

rationale behind them.

From the expert review we got a good idea of what solution to filament storage they use at
NOVA Fab Labs, and we adapted our design accordingly. We kept the actual storage system
very close to the 3D printers for the convenience of everyone in the classroom in the design.
This decision was based on how they use boxes close to the printers at NOVA Fab Labs, and
the convenience that it brings. We switched to dowels/pipes that can be screwed into the shelf
using 3D printed connections in the design, also for ease of access which was emphasized in
the feedback of the expert reviewer and what they do in their labs. We switched from wooden
dowels to cheaper and lighter PVC, which will work better for our design in this context, and
which is validated by the use of the cheapest possible materials for storage in the labs.

Conclusion Reflect briefly on integrating STEM principles into your project, focusing on the
impact on your design process and the challenges addressed.

 We used STEM principles such as ability to investigate and falsify and using mathematical
calculation and engineering methods to inform the design requirements and the design itself.

modularity of the design.
